title: Massachusetts's 6th Congressional District Election, 2026
description: The 2026 election for Massachusetts's 6th Congressional District is an open-seat race following incumbent Rep. Seth Moulton's decision to run for the U.S. Senate instead of seeking re-election. The district covers northeastern Massachusetts, including the North Shore communities of Lynn, Salem, Gloucester, and parts of the Merrimack Valley. With Moulton's departure, a competitive Democratic primary has emerged, featuring candidates with experience in government, business, and activism. The district has been represented by Democrats since 2015 and is rated Safe/Solid D by major nonpartisan forecasters, making the Democratic primary the de facto decisive contest.
polling_note: No public, nonpartisan opinion polls were found for the 2026 MA-06 general election. Several internal campaign polls have been released but lack independent verification or full methodological disclosure.

candidates.name: Dan Koh
candidates.summary: Dan Koh is a former White House senior aide and former chief of staff to Boston Mayor and U.S. Labor Secretary Marty Walsh. He has raised the most money of any candidate in the race, approximately $3.5 million, and emphasizes his experience in government at the federal and local levels. Koh previously ran for Congress in Massachusetts's 3rd District in 2018, narrowly losing the Democratic primary to Rep. Lori Trahan.

candidates.name: Jamie Belsito
candidates.summary: Jamie Belsito is the Topsfield Town Moderator and a former state representative who served the 4th Essex District from 2021 to 2023 before the district was eliminated by redistricting. She is the founder of the Maternal Mental Health Leadership Alliance, a nonprofit advocating for maternal mental health policy. Belsito frames her campaign around rolling back what she calls 'Reagan Economics' and has taken the People's Pledge to reject PAC, billionaire, and corporate executive contributions.

candidates.name: John Beccia
candidates.summary: John Beccia is a business executive and adjunct law professor at Boston University who has loaned his campaign $2 million and raised approximately $400,000. He describes himself as a political outsider with experience in financial services regulation, consumer protection, and business creation. Beccia emphasizes 'kitchen table issues' such as the economy, education, and healthcare, and says he entered the race out of frustration with the direction of federal policy.

candidates.name: Beth Andres-Beck
candidates.summary: Beth Andres-Beck is a software engineer with 20 years of experience who was the first candidate to enter the race. They use they/them pronouns and frame their campaign around regulating artificial intelligence, which they describe as an urgent and far-reaching issue reshaping the economy and workforce. Andres-Beck supports Medicare for All, holding Donald Trump accountable, and abolishing ICE, and argues that their technology background sets them apart from other candidates.

candidates.name: Rachel Creemers
candidates.summary: Rachel Creemers is a labor rights advocate who has worked with the American Postal Workers Union and the National Labor Relations Board. She centers her campaign on a proposed Workers' Bill of Rights, aiming to expand job security, stability, and workers' protections. Creemers also prioritizes climate change legislation, public broadcasting, and housing as a human right, emphasizing affordability near transit stations.

candidates.name: Mariah Lancaster
candidates.summary: Mariah Lancaster is a veterinarian and progressive activist running for Congress in her first bid for elected office. She emphasizes universal healthcare, equitable education, and clean energy as central campaign pillars. Lancaster secured a spot on the Democratic primary ballot and has been endorsed by local grassroots organizations.

candidates.name: Micah Jones
candidates.summary: Micah Jones is a U.S. Army veteran who served in Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division and later worked in securities enforcement litigation. He is the only Republican candidate in the race and emphasizes bipartisanship, congressional accountability, and insider trading reform. Jones lives in Essex and says his top priority is strengthening rules to prevent members of Congress from trading stocks based on non-public information.

forecast.rationale: No verified public general-election polling is available. The forecast relies on structural district context: MA-06 is rated Safe/Solid Democratic by major nonpartisan forecasters, Democrats have held the seat since 2015, and the open-seat competition is concentrated in the Democratic primary (described as the de facto decisive contest). The district's underlying partisan lean in northeastern Massachusetts strongly favors Democrats in the general election. Confidence is medium because there are no independent public polls, the seat is open, and a credible Republican candidate (Micah Jones) is running, but the district's fundamentals point to a safe Democratic hold.
